posts.title: Research: Pacing (Dong & Li 2026)
posts.caption:
Start a marathon more than 5% faster than your average pace, and 26.6% of runners hit the wall. Start near your average pace: 1.5%.

Dong and Li looked at the split times of 78,912 Boston Marathon finishers. Even pacing was the most common pattern (47.9%) and was linked to faster finishes. The authors suggest restraint in the early miles and structured pacing practice, especially for newer marathoners.

Limits: this is observational, so even pacing may mark fitness rather than cause speed. Boston qualifiers only, on one point-to-point, net-downhill course, with no training or weather data.

How fast do you go out in the first 10K?

Source: Dong Q, Li Z. Pacing strategy patterns and performance outcomes in marathon running. PLOS ONE, 2026. doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0352808

Save this for your next build.

#raceproof #marathontraining #marathonrunner #bostonmarathon #runningcommunity
altText: Research post on pacing. Start more than 5% faster than your average pace: 26.6% hit the wall. Start near your average pace: 1.5%. Dong and Li 2026, PLOS ONE.
What they found: 47.9% ran an even pace. Strong positive splitters were 59.5 minutes slower on average than even pacers. 82.0% of sub-3:00 runners paced evenly, 19.6% of runners over 4:30.
Bar chart of how often runners hit the wall: 26.6% of those who started more than 5% faster than average pace, 1.5% of those who started near average pace. A link, not proof.
The study: 78,912 Boston Marathon finishers, 2015 to 2017, sorted into four pacing patterns: even 47.9%, mild positive 31.9%, strong positive 12.2%, variable 8.0%.
Two quotes from the authors recommending pacing discipline, restraint early in the race, and structured pacing practice for novice marathoners.
Our take, not a finding of the study: know your goal pace before race day by holding it in long runs on tired legs. Example card: Pacing, 3 goal-pace long runs done, Ready.
Source and thanks: Pacing strategy patterns and performance outcomes in marathon running, Qizheng Dong and Zaidong Li, PLOS ONE 2026, doi 10.1371/journal.pone.0352808. Save this for your next build.
flags: Calendar hook said 'Start on pace: 1.5%'. The paper's comparison group is runners whose early pace was near their average, so the slide says 'Start near your average pace: 1.5%'.
Slide 5 quotes come from the paper's Discussion and Conclusion (read on journals.plos.org); the Research library row has no 'authors advise' text. No numbers taken from outside the library row.

posts.title: Product: What Raceproof checks
posts.caption:
Your plan covers the miles. Raceproof checks the rest.

Seven things race day will test: gut, hydration, heat, terrain, durability, pacing and taper. Five are automatic from your watch. Gut and hydration take a 15-second log after key sessions. Each one shows as Ready, Building or Gap against your race.

altText: What Raceproof checks. Your plan covers the miles. We check the rest. Seven pillars: gut, hydration, heat, terrain, durability, pacing, taper. Coming spring 2027.
Gut, quick log: the carbs you've practiced vs what your race needs. Example: 55 of 80 g/h proven, Building.
Hydration, quick log: your sweat rate and sodium vs your race plan, from weigh-ins or an hDrop or lab sweat test. Example: no sweat rate yet, Gap.
Heat, automatic: sessions trained in heat vs your race forecast. Example: 9 runs above 80°F, Ready.
Terrain, automatic: climbing and descending vs your course. Example: longest descent trained 3,500 ft, Building.
Durability, automatic: heart rate and pace late in your long sessions. Example: HR drifts after 2:40, Building.
Pacing, automatic: goal pace held in training, and for how long. Example: 3 goal-pace long runs done, Ready.
Taper, automatic: training load and sleep in your final weeks. Example: sleep 7.4 h average, Building. Join the waitlist, link in bio.

posts.title: Research blog: Carbs per hour in a marathon (article 1)
posts.caption:
60 to 90 g of carbs an hour. Most marathoners take 35.

Your finish time sets your target: about 60 g/h for a 2 to 3 hour race, up to 90 g/h when you're out longer, from mixed sugars and a gut you've trained. At the 2022 Seville Marathon, runners averaged 35 g/h and only 9% reached that range.

The gut adapts. Two weeks of practice cut gut symptoms by about 60% in one small lab trial.

Studies: ADA, DC and ACSM 2016; Burke et al. 2011; Jeukendrup 2014 (Gatorade Sports Science Institute); Jiménez-Alfageme et al. 2025 (survey of 160 runners); Smyth 2021 (observational race data); Norte et al. 2026 and Costa et al. 2017 (small lab trials).

Full article: raceproof.ai/blog/carbs-per-hour-marathon (link in bio). Save this for your next build.

#raceproof #marathontraining #racefueling #guttraining #sportsnutrition
altText: Slide 1: 60 to 90 g of carbs an hour. Most marathoners take 35. Only 9% at the 2022 Seville Marathon reached the range.
Slide 2: Your finish time sets the target. 2 to 3 hours: about 60 g/h. Over 2.5 to 3 hours: up to 90 g/h from mixed sugars.
Slide 3: Seville Marathon 2022: 35 g/h average, 41.3% under 30 g/h, 9.0% in the 60 to 90 g/h range.
Slide 4: 28% of men and 17% of women hit the wall, starting around 29 to 30 km, costing about half an hour.
Slide 5: Critical power after 3 hours of cycling: 236 W on water, 257 W at 60 g/h, 266 W at 120 g/h, fresh 277 W.
Slide 6: Two weeks of gut training: 60% fewer gut symptoms with gels, plus 5.2% on a 1-hour run test, placebo minus 2.1%.
Slide 7: Our take: pick your target from your finish time. Gut readiness row: 55 g/h practiced, target 80, Building.

posts.title: Pain: Gut (96% at a 100-miler)
posts.caption:
96% of runners at a 100-miler had at least one gut symptom. For 36% of the runners who dropped out, gut trouble was one of the reasons.

Most symptoms were mild, and nausea was the one behind most gut-related drops. The fix starts in training: take your race fuel on every long run and build toward race-day carbs a little at a time.

Join the waitlist. Link in bio.

Source: Stuempfle & Hoffman 2015, Journal of Sports Sciences (272 runners at the Western States 100, self-reported after the race).

#raceproof #ultrarunning #100miler #guttraining #racefueling
altText: 96% of runners at a 100-miler had gut symptoms. For 36% of dropouts, it was a reason to stop. A grid of 100 dots with 96 filled orange. Any GI symptom, mostly mild, Western States 100. Source: Stuempfle and Hoffman 2015.
The fix: Gut, 55 of 80 g/h proven, Building. Take your race fuel on every long run. Add a little every week or two until race-day carbs feel normal. That's what Raceproof checks, every week.
